what_it_does: Modern processors contain secure, isolated execution environments — think of them as walled-off vaults inside the chip — that are meant to protect sensitive code even from a compromised operating system. Two widely used vaults are Intel SGX and AMD SEV. This paper addresses a subtle weakness: when secret-dependent code takes two different branches (think of an if/else that branches differently depending on a password), the two paths often execute a different number of instructions and therefore take measurably different amounts of time. An attacker who can precisely time these differences can infer the secret. The authors build a compiler tool that automatically finds such unbalanced branches and rewrites the machine instructions so both paths look identical to a timer — inserting dummy operations, shuffling instruction order, or interleaving the two paths — without changing the program's output. The contribution is that this hardening happens automatically at the compiler level and works at the granularity of individual machine instructions, which is finer than source-level defenses that miss microarchitectural timing gaps.
